title: The soul receives contraries and so is not the body's entelechy
pass_a_gloss: Bodily substance is receptive of contraries in part, but not according to the form. If the difference according to the form is changed, the being itself is changed. Therefore substance according to the form is not receptive of contraries, but substance according to the underlying subject — that is, the bodily. So the soul cannot in any way be the entelechy of the body; it is a self-complete, incorporeal substance, for it receives contraries in part — vice and virtue — which the form could not receive. Further, if the soul were entelechy it would be immovable in itself and moved only accidentally; yet even if beauty, being immovable, moves us, what moves must have a nature to move, and the body is not self-moving apart from the soul.
pass_b_english: A body can take on opposed qualities in its matter, but not in its form: change the form and you change the thing. Contraries therefore sit in the underlying body, not in the form as such. That is why the soul cannot be the body's entelechy. It stands as its own complete, bodiless substance, able to receive virtue and vice — opposed states no mere form could host. Call the soul an entelechy and you make it motionless in itself, moved only by accident; yet the body does not move itself. Whatever first moves it must come from the soul.
